title: Social Identity Theory and Group Dynamics
text:
Social Identity Theory posits that an individual's sense of self is derived not only from personal attributes but also significantly from the groups to which they belong. This theory suggests that people are motivated to maintain a positive social identity, leading them to categorize both themselves (the in-group) and others (the out-group). The perceived status of the group becomes integral to self-esteem.

The formation of these boundaries often results in ingroup favoritism, where members naturally tend to view their own group's characteristics as superior. Conversely, this positive bias can lead to stereotyping and derogation of outgroups. These mechanisms are key drivers behind prejudice and intergroup conflict, suggesting that managing social comparison is a fundamental aspect of human sociology.

Analyzing these dynamics reveals how group affiliation influences perceptions of reality and morality. Understanding the psychological underpinnings of collective behavior allows for insights into systemic biases within various communities.
